newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF says Nomura head responsible for scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF says Nomura head responsible for scandal.

text.p: The president of Nomura Securities Co Ltd is responsible for the scandal in which it is embroiled concerning suspected illegal dealings regardless of whether the company itself was involved, a senior Ministry of Finance (MOF) official told Reuters on Wednesday.
Even if Nomura's president, Hideo Sakamaki, did not know about the deals, top management must take responsibility for a lack of supervision of the company's business, he said.
He also said the ministry has told Sakamaki that Nomura must work out a programme to avoid a recurrence of such scandals.

Nomura said last Thursday that two of its directors apparently made discretionary transactions and moved profits raised from Nomura's own funds into a corporate client's account. Both actions violate the Securities Exchange Law.
Japan banned brokers from making discretionary transactions with clients in 1991, after the securities industry was hit by scandals over favoured clients being compensated for losses.
Japanese media have reported that the Nomura corporate client concerned was run by the brother of a former "sokaiya" racketeer, but Nomura said it could not confirm those reports.

Sokaiya extort money from companies by threatening to disturb shareholders' meetings or by offering to prevent disruption of the proceedings. Japanese commercial law has prohibited paying off racketeers since 1982.

The MOF official said that while the ministry will wait to see the outcome of the investigation by Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), it was focusing on whether Nomura had violated the commercial code, rather than the securities law.
If the SESC investigation finds that such payoffs were made to a racketeer, the ministry will take strict administrative penalties against Nomura, the MOF official said.
He said that it would probably take some time, however, for the SESC to conclude its investigation, though he declined to speculate on how long.
He said that privately he did not believe that the president and other top executives in Nomura had knowledge of the apparently irregular dealings.
He added that he did not believe the latest scandal involving Nomura would not have a major impact on Japan's stock market as a whole.
Nomura said the two company executives involved in the scandal have resigned as managing directors but will stay on with the company to help investigate details of the incident.
A Nomura spokesman said Sakamaki has said he will decide what he should do regarding his position after the SESC investigation has been completed.
